why: Gregory VII (Hildebrand) was pope from 1073 to 1085. He excommunicated and deposed the German emperor Henry IV and made papal supremacy a working claim. Later Protestants blame him for the papacy's claims, so Bengel and the English writers name him as the start of the 'Hildebrandine' papacy.
reason: He has papal acts in his own name on his home shelf, founded no movement, and two later Protestant traditions name him repeatedly in their own voice.
doubts: Both later voices are hostile, and each tradition's count rests mostly on one author (Bengel in German and English; Barlow's Brutum Fulmen plus one Church of England tract). Many counted hits use the name Hildebrand; I checked Barlow and Bengel and these name the pope. Namesakes (John Hildebrand of Ephrata, Joachim Hildebrand and others) were excluded in the input notes. OCR reads 'Gregory. Vl.' for VII in Barlow. Mirbt is a modern editor's collection of documents; the home quote is the 1076 prayer to Peter, set in his own name. Bengel line 21177 uses 'Hildebrand' as a byword (Zosimus 'an early Hildebrand') and names Gregory VII only by figure; the count holds without it, since the German file names him in body text at 31538, 31585, 32393 and 34195, and 34195 can take its place. Bellarmine, Notes of the Church 14580 quotes Bellarmine's own list of saints, so the words are his; it still counts, and Restoration is 9 without it anyway. The movement carries his name ('Gregorian Reform'), but the census dates it from Leo IX's circle around 1049, before his pontificate, so he is not its founder.
